content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Robert Weber (E047) requests admin access to Source Code.

The team memory has 6 notes. Five notes say he's a full-time Payroll Specialist, and one note (Security DB) says he's a contractor with basic security training.

Conflicting information: 5 notes say full_time Payroll Specialist, 1 note says contractor with basic security training.

Let me apply the policy:
- If full_time Payroll Specialist: max is write (admin only if role owns system - Source Code owned by Engineer, not Payroll Specialist). So requested admin > max write → grant write.
- If contractor with basic security training: max is read (contractor read, or write with advanced training). Requested admin > max read → grant read.

Which to believe? The majority of notes (5 out of 6) across multiple systems (HR/IT? Actually the notes are from different agents: note 1 (probably HR), note 2 (IT), note 3 (Finance), note 4 (Compliance), note 5 (Facilities), note 6 (Security). The Security note contradicts the others.

Hmm. This is a conflict. The typical approach for the Approver: weigh evidence. Five independent DBs confirm full-time Payroll Specialist; one (Security) says contractor with basic training. Most consistent view is he's full-time Payroll Specialist.

Given the majority, grant write? The request is admin. Max is write. So grant write.

Actually, let me think carefully. The notes come from agents each representing their DB. The HR agent, IT agent, Finance agent, Compliance agent, Facilities agent, Security agent. Five say full-time Payroll Specialist. One (Security) says contractor. The preponderance of evidence supports full-time Payroll Specialist.

I'll decide write.

Reason: Employee is full-time Payroll Specialist per majority of records; Source Code is owned by Engineer role, so admin not permitted; maximum is write; requested admin exceeds max, so grant write.
